doc.title: Christian McBride interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

title: Number Two Express: diversity, guests and evolution
summary: The new album reflects his musical diversity, with Chick Corea, Jack DeJohnette, Kenny Garrett, Gary Bartz, Steve Nelson and Kenny Barron; recording is like a growing tree.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Tell us about the new record coming out in just a few days.

Yeah the new record is called “Number Two Express” and I’m so excited, I’m so excited, because you know the new album represents me where I am now musically — things I like to listen to and things I like to go for and the things that I would like to eventually have the band get into. You know I’ve always been about diversity. You know you can’t be in just one bag. And I try to make a conscious effort for my band to play you know lots of blues and some progressive stuff maybe some things leaning to a funk, and then playing all the standards. You know, cover all the areas, because the legacy of jazz is so huge, I mean you just can’t stick to one part of it. And especially people’s, the general public’s ignorance level toward jazz is so high you have to let them hear more than one

bag so they’ll know what it’s all about. And you know on the new album I have Chick Corea playing acoustic and electric piano and one of the best things about that was him and Jack DeJohnette got to play together again, because Jack is on the album also. And they hadn’t worked together. They told me they’d maybe played together maybe three or four times since 1969. And it was such a thrill for me to have them record on my new CD. And Kenny Garret is on it as well playing alto saxophone. And on the other half of the album, Gary Bartz is playing alto saxophone, Steve Nelson is playing vibes, Kenny Barron is playing piano and Jack is on drums. And we’re really stretching out. See on my first album, “Getting To It” was really a rootsy type album. You know I see recording as a tree. You know, you make your first album, those are your roots. And each album something grows out of that. So the second record is different from the first record and you know the third record I’m sure will be different from the second and so forth and so on. So you know, evolution.
